intro: Three pictures the exam keeps coming back to. Drag a score along the normal curve and watch its z score and percentile rank change, with the 68-95-99.7 bands drawn under it. Drag one value of a small data set far away and watch the mean chase it while the median stays put. Then set a correlation and see what r = 0.3 and r = −0.9 really look like.
howItWorks:
Every number is computed by the course's statistics library (the same code the practice questions use). A z score is (score − mean) ÷ standard deviation. The percent below a score at a whole standard deviation uses the 68-95-99.7 rule exactly: 34% between the mean and 1 SD, 13.5% between 1 and 2 SD, 2.35% between 2 and 3 SD, 0.15% beyond 3 SD, the same on each side. Between whole marks the lab also shows the exact share under the normal curve; the exam only asks for whole marks, worked by hand.

The data sets and scatterplots are invented for practice. Pearson's r is computed from the points drawn, so what you see is what r measures. The words strong (|r| of .7 or more), moderate (.4 to .7) and weak (.1 to .4) are a common rule of thumb, not a fixed standard.

contexts.lead: An intelligence test is given to a large, representative sample.
A college entrance test is taken by thousands of high school students.
In an invented lab study, a researcher measures how many words people recall from a list.
A student takes two tests in the same week.
Two classes give final exams scored on different scales.
In an invented survey, students report how many text messages they sent in the last hour.
In an invented sleep study, researchers record how many minutes each volunteer takes to fall asleep.
In an invented memory study, participants recall words from a list of 30.
A researcher surveys teenagers about screen time before bed and how long they sleep.
contexts.claim: Can the researcher conclude that screen time before bed changes how long teenagers sleep?
contexts.right: No. A correlation cannot show cause; a third variable such as stress could affect both.
contexts.rightWhy: Right. The researcher measured both variables without assigning anyone a screen time, so a third variable (stress, homework, an early school start) could drive both, or the direction could run the other way.
contexts.wrong: Yes, because the two variables are clearly related.
contexts.thirdWhy: Stress, for example, could both keep a teenager on a phone and cut their sleep.

contexts.lead: A teacher records, for each student, the hours spent studying and the score on the unit test.
contexts.claim: Can the teacher conclude that studying more causes higher scores?
contexts.right: No. This is correlational data; interest in the subject, for example, could raise both.
contexts.rightWhy: Right. The teacher did not assign study hours, so a third variable such as interest or prior knowledge could explain both. An experiment would randomly assign study time.
contexts.wrong: Yes, because students who studied more scored higher.
contexts.thirdWhy: Interest in the subject, for example, could make a student both study more and score higher.

contexts.lead: A researcher measures adults' shoe size and their score on a memory test.
contexts.claim: Can the researcher conclude that shoe size affects memory?
contexts.right: No. A correlation never shows cause, and any link here is likely a coincidence or a third variable.
contexts.rightWhy: Right. Whatever r is, a correlational study cannot show cause; a third variable (age, sex) or chance could produce the pattern.
contexts.wrong: Yes, because the points follow a pattern.
contexts.thirdWhy: Age or sex, for example, could relate to both foot size and test scores.
